task: find the current azure blob storage pricing tiers and what each is for
text:
## What you asked
Current Azure Blob Storage pricing tiers and what each one is for.

## The tiers

Five, and they trade storage cost against access cost in a straight line. Prices below are East US, locally-redundant (LRS), pay-as-you-go, first 50 TB — pulled today from Microsoft's pricing page.

| Tier | Storage /GB/mo | Cost to read 1 GB | Min. stay | Time to get data |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Premium** | $0.15 | free (cheapest transactions) | none | milliseconds, consistently low |
| **Hot** | $0.0184 | free | none | milliseconds |
| **Cool** | $0.010 | $0.01 + higher per-op | 30 days | milliseconds |
| **Cold** | $0.0036 | $0.03 + much higher per-op | 90 days | milliseconds |
| **Archive** | $0.002 | $0.02 + very high per-op | 180 days | up to 15 hours |

**What each is for**
- **Premium** — latency-sensitive, transaction-heavy workloads (interactive apps, analytics with many small reads). You pay ~8x hot for storage but ~1/30th per read operation.
- **Hot** — anything in active use. The default, and the right answer for most workloads.
- **Cool** — short-term backup, disaster recovery, data you touch occasionally but need instantly.
- **Cold** — older datasets you almost never open but can't wait hours for.
- **Archive** — long-term retention, compliance, raw data you keep because you must. Offline: you cannot read it until you "rehydrate" it, which takes hours.

## The traps worth knowing
- **Early deletion penalty.** Delete, overwrite, or move a blob before its minimum stay and you're billed for the remaining days anyway. Archive at 180 days is the expensive one.
- **Retrieval fees undo the savings fast.** Cool saves ~$0.008/GB/month over Hot, but costs $0.01/GB to read. Read that data more than about once a month and Cool is more expensive than Hot. Same math on Cold at roughly half a read per month.
- **Archive doesn't support zone redundancy** — LRS, GRS, RA-GRS only.

## Two things that cut the bill further
- **Reserved capacity** — commit to 100 TB or 1 PB for 1 or 3 years. 100 TB Hot drops from ~$1,884/mo pay-as-you-go to $1,545 (1-year) or $1,244 (3-year), roughly a third off.
- **Smart tier** — Microsoft moves blobs between Hot/Cool/Cold automatically based on actual usage, so you stop guessing. You pay the underlying tier's rate plus a small monthly monitoring fee per 10,000 objects. Only available on zone-redundant accounts (ZRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS). The monitoring fee didn't render for the region I scraped, so I don't have that number.

**My recommendation:** default everything to Hot, then put a lifecycle rule on it — auto-move to Cool at 30 days untouched, Archive at 180. That captures most of the savings without you having to predict access patterns. Smart tier is the lower-effort version of the same idea if you're on zone-redundant storage.

Prices vary by region and redundancy — these are estimates from the public page, not a quote. Tell me your region and redundancy setting and I'll pull the exact numbers.

task: explain the difference between cross-validation and a holdout test set
text:
Both are answers to the same question: *how do I know my model works on data it has never seen?* They differ in how many times you ask.

**Holdout test set** — split your data once. Train on ~80%, lock away ~20%, and only look at the locked-away part at the end. One split, one score.

**Cross-validation** — split the data into, say, 5 equal chunks. Train 5 times, each time holding out a different chunk as the test. You get 5 scores and average them. Every row gets used for training *and* for testing, just never in the same run.

**The infra analogy:** a holdout test is testing your failover once, from one region, on one day — fast, and if it fails you learn something real. Cross-validation is running the failover drill five times across five regions and averaging the results. Far more confidence that the result wasn't a fluke of which region you happened to pick, at five times the compute.

| | Holdout test set | Cross-validation |
|---|---|---|
| Splits | 1 | typically 5 or 10 |
| Cost | 1× training run | 5–10× training runs |
| Result | a single number | an average, plus a spread |
| Main weakness | got a lucky/unlucky split? you'd never know | expensive; and you can overuse it until it flatters you |
| Best when | data is plentiful; final sign-off | data is scarce; comparing model options |

**The part that actually matters in practice:** they aren't rivals — the good setups use both, for different jobs.

- Cross-validation is for **choosing** — which model, which settings. You'll run it dozens of times while tuning.
- The holdout test set is for **final judgment** — the number you report. It works only because you touched it once. Every time you peek at it and adjust something, it quietly becomes part of your training data and stops being an honest estimate.

That's the discipline: tune with cross-validation, then break the seal on the holdout exactly once. It's the same reason you don't let the person who wrote the firewall rules be the only one who audits them.

One caveat worth knowing: if your data has a time order — stock prices, logs, anything sequential — plain cross-validation cheats. It trains on Thursday to predict Wednesday. For time-ordered data you need the walk-forward variant, which only ever trains on the past. Relevant to Tickr, if that comes up.

text:
## What you asked
Current Azure Blob Storage tiers and what each one is for.

## The five tiers

| Tier | Use it for | Minimum stay | Retrieval speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hot** | Data in active use — read/written regularly | none | instant |
| **Cool** | Infrequent access, but still needs to be online — short-term backup, recent archives | 30 days | instant |
| **Cold** | Rarely touched, but must come back fast when it is — older datasets, long-tail records | 90 days | instant |
| **Archive** | Compliance retention, long-term backup you hope never to read | 180 days | **hours** (up to 15) |
| **Smart** | You don't want to decide — Azure moves data between Hot/Cool/Cold automatically based on actual usage | n/a | instant |

**Premium block blob** is a separate thing — not a tier you set per file, but a different account type (~$0.15/GB) for workloads needing consistently low latency and very high transaction rates.

## What they cost
East US, locally-redundant, standard account, first 50 TB/month. Pulled from Microsoft's live retail pricing API today.

| | Hot | Cool | Cold | Archive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Storage** (per GB/mo) | $0.0208 | $0.0152 | $0.0036 | $0.00099 |
| **Reads** (per 10k) | $0.004 | $0.01 | $0.10 | $5.00 |
| **Writes** (per 10k) | $0.05 | $0.10 | $0.18 | $0.10 |
| **Retrieval** (per GB) | free | $0.01 | $0.03 | $0.02 |
| **Availability SLA** | 99.9% | 99% | 99% | 99% |

The trade is always the same: each step down cuts storage cost and raises the cost of touching the data.

## Two things worth knowing
- **Cool is barely a discount in East US** — 27% off Hot, while Cold is 83% off and Archive 95% off. If data is genuinely cold, skipping Cool and going straight to Cold saves far more. In other regions (Central US, West US 2) Cool is cheaper, so this is region-specific.
- **Early deletion is charged.** Delete or move a blob before its minimum stay and you pay the remainder anyway — pro-rated. Archive is the sharp edge: delete after 45 days and you're billed for the other 135.

Two caveats: prices vary meaningfully by region and redundancy setting (geo-redundant roughly doubles storage cost), and Archive isn't available on zone-redundant accounts at all.

task: explain the difference between cross-validation and a holdout test set
text:
No existing ML note in your Learning folder — this would be a new one.

## The problem both solve

You've built a model. It scores 94% on the data you trained it on — but that number is worthless, because the model has effectively memorised those examples. You need to know how it performs on data it has *never seen*. Both techniques manufacture "unseen data" out of the data you already have.

## Holdout test set

Split your data once — say 80% to train on, 20% locked in a drawer. Train, then score against the drawer. One split, one number.

**Infra analogy:** a single pre-prod smoke test. You test in one environment, it passes, you ship.

## Cross-validation

Split the data into (typically) five equal chunks. Train five times — each run holds out a different chunk as the test set. You end up with five scores, and you look at the average *and* the spread.

**Infra analogy:** instead of testing failover into one availability zone, you rotate the test through every zone. If it only works in one, you find out. If the five results are 91/92/90/93/91, you trust it. If they're 94/71/88/62/90, your model is unstable and the single-split number would have lied to you.

## The comparison

| | Holdout | Cross-validation |
|---|---|---|
| Splits | One | Typically 5 or 10 |
| Cost to run | 1× training | 5–10× training |
| What you get | A single score | Average **plus** a stability signal |
| Weakness | Result depends on the luck of the split | Expensive; can't be reused as a final verdict |
| Best on | Large datasets, expensive models | Small datasets, model selection |

## They aren't rivals — use both

This is the part that trips people up. The standard practice:

1. **Hold out a test set once, at the very start, and don't touch it.** This is your final exam.
2. **Cross-validate on everything that's left** while you're choosing algorithms and tuning settings.
3. **Touch the test set exactly once**, at the end, to report the honest number.

The reason for the discipline: every time you look at a score and change the model because of it, you leak information about that data into your model. Cross-validation is where you're *allowed* to iterate. The test set is the one thing you haven't contaminated — and it stops being trustworthy the moment you tune against it.

**The one-line version:** cross-validation tells you how to *build* the model; the holdout test set tells you how good the model you built actually is.

---

Want this saved to your Learning notes in the vault? It'd pair naturally with a follow-on note on data leakage, which is the failure mode this whole discipline exists to prevent — and it's directly relevant to Tickr, where time-ordered market data makes random splits actively dangerous.
